The proposed method combines the advantages of Brzozowski's regular expression algebra and the approach using automata-based inequalities solving, while also introducing a novel algorithm for solving set containment checks using Brzozowski's algebra. It has been implemented in the HOL4 proof assistant and verified through its effectiveness in solving various inequality problems, demonstrating its potential utility in theoretical computer science, particularly in the analysis of programs that utilize data defined by regular expressions, as well as in the verification of privacy concepts in data anonymization processes.

We provide a detailed explanation of how to compute crossing-symmetric ward identities in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence, specifically within the bulk bulk bulk three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space. We explain how to integrate by parts within the bulk, utilizing the bulk bulk bulk geodesic distance, as well as how to define the operator product expansion within the CFT at the conformal boundary. We also discuss the connection between the OPE and the four-point geodesic bulk quantity, utilizing the bulk bulk bulk geodesic distance.

To greatly increase the field of view in broad-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a new concept: a multiple LE (MULE) design. This innovative configuration consists of four LE lenses with their foci overlaid and a sensitive area that is effectively expanded 100-fold with minimal loss in signal, as evaluated using simulations. Based on the theoretical gains, a MULE-based monitor with a 40deg x 40deg field of view should be capable of detecting a signal-to-noise ratio of 10:1 in just 10 milliseconds per image, and the development of a suitable prototype is deemed feasible using existing production techniques for LE optics.

To investigate the impact of velocity information on dark matter halo mass distribution, a new proxy called the cosmic speed field has been proposed. Initially, it is crucial to establish the physical basis for this new quantity, in order to determine its practical uses in research. By examining the underlying causes of cosmic speed field's correlation with the halo mass, we aim to evaluate its potential value for mapping halo masses. To accomplish this, we will explore the cosmic speed field's ability to learn through a deep learning algorithm and compare its effectiveness to a established quantity called the total density field. To determine the cosmic speed field's capability to serve as a precursor for halo mass, we will conduct an analysis of its statistical properties, assess its ability to resolve halo masses, and examine its relationship with the halo bias. Through a mock dataset constructed from the Planck cosmology, we will evaluate the cosmic speed field's potential to learn through a deep learning algorithm and compare its performance to the total density field. Based on the results, we will assess the cosmic speed field's ability to reconstruct halo masses and examine its resolution limits. To further investigate the cosmic speed field's capability to learn through a deep learning algorithm, we will conduct an analysis of its statistical properties, assess its ability to resolve halo masses, and examine its relationship with the halo bias. Through a range of halo masses, we will examine the cosmic speed field's ability to reconstruct halo masses and compare its performance to the total density field. Based on the results, we will

This study proposes a novel method that combines atomic interferometry with the Meissner effect of a superconducting material to sensitively detect even the smallest changes in a magnetic field. Unlike traditional atomic interferometry, this approach doesn't require a uniform magnetic field, eliminating the need for complicated magnetic field shielding. By placing a superconducting material near the atomic beam, this method can instantly sense any changes in the magnetic field by measuring the changes in the beam's oscillations, even if they occur outside the measurement area. If the area of interest is surrounded by the superconducting material to form a hole with the desired shape, this hole's boundary will take the form of a loop with a known cross-sectional area, creating a uniform magnetic field within it by inducing a current when an external magnetic field is applied. The research team demonstrated this concept by building a setup using rubidium atoms and a superconducting ring to detect changes in the magnetic field within a hole with a cross-sectional area of about 1 cm^2. The results showed that this method could sense changes in the magnetic field as small as 10^-12 tesla.

A comprehensive quantum theory has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states resulting from the interaction between localized magnetic moments and superconducting substrates. This theory, based on the initial principles and excluding the use of the Bloch equation, has been applied to individual manganese adatoms and dimers deposited on a niobium surface. Theoretical findings have been compared with experimental data obtained through tunneling spectroscopy, demonstrating a high level of consistency and accuracy. The developed approach has further been employed to examine the spin-polarized electron properties of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states, in addition to their influence on the substrate's superconducting properties. The results have been found to be in excellent agreement with experimental outcomes, paving the way for its potential use in various quantum materials.

This study proposes a new method that combines a deep learning algorithm with a distance-based outlier detection method to accurately identify outlier skin carcinoma samples. Following the integration, a dimensionality reduction technique is employed to further enhance the proposed model by dealing with complex feature spaces. The proposed framework is then tested on two publicly available datasets: PHENOCAM and SKFS. The results demonstrate that the combined approach, utilizing a distance metric, achieves the highest accuracy compared to other methods. Furthermore, the study conducts an in-depth analysis of the outlier detection technique by examining its ability to identify truly outlier samples and comparing it to alternative methods. The proposed framework's performance is found to be highly accurate in both true outlier identification and overall classification, as evidenced by accuracy scores of 97.1% and 97.8% on the PHENOCAM and SKFS datasets, respectively.

Determining the energy of incident vector bosons is crucial in particle physics experiments, particularly in the case of the TeV-scale W and Z bosons. Since the energy measurement of decay particles is imperfect, especially for muons, a precise method is necessary to estimate this energy. We propose a new approach, the "Central Value" method, which utilizes the most accurate particle energy estimates, typically those of electrons, as the standard for calculating the vector boson energy. By applying this method, we anticipate a significant improvement in the W and Z mass measurements, potentially reducing the uncertainty from 0.10% to 0.02% or less, depending on the future particle colliders' capabilities.

We bring together Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser in the same venue to address a longstanding issue in semantics. Our gathering focuses on the concept of a sound mirror reflection, a theoretical tool that hinges on the use of modal logic to define truth within formal systems. We begin within the framework of a proven, yet uncertain, formal system known as PM, which we utilize for our arguments. Tarski's approach to defining truth through a mirror reflection aligns with his earlier work on semantic concepts, but we believe an improvement is possible. Building on our previous paper, we outline a direct definition of truth that bypasses the use of mirror reflections entirely. This new approach leverages a component of PM that was previously underutilized, specifically the recursive syntax rules for formulas. We term this definition "straight reflection" in contrast to the conventional "sound mirror reflection" definition. Our analysis demonstrates that both definitions are equivalent in terms of their logical consequences, as well as their applicability to modeling truth within formal models. This achievement extends the applicability of truth definitions to more diverse logical systems, some of which may not meet the required soundness criteria. Notably, we apply our findings to a specific case involving a famous theorem by Godel, which states that any consistent formal system capable of arithmetic is not itself provable within that system. This paper examines the concept of an invariant surface in dynamical systems and proves that, except for linear centers and circles, there are no invariant straight lines for planar systems whose vector field F has constant or linearly varying in magnitude with respect to the radius, components. Moreover, we extend this result to show that only circles and linear centers are invariant for systems whose vector field F is linear or has a polynomial representation with respect to polar coordinates, concluding that, except for circles and linear centers, there are no invariant straight lines for systems whose vector field F is analytic in the radius.

This study proposes an inverse problem where a material parameter of an active structure with an attached acoustic chamber is determined based on measurement data from a sensor within the chamber. A key aspect is the ability to use acoustic output as an input to the structure, differing from existing research on passive structures. The proposed method utilizes a bio-inspired neural network, specifically a genetic algorithm optimized extreme learning machine (GA-ELM), in conjunction with a physics-based model to solve the inverse problem. To verify the proposal's efficacy, simulations were conducted on a sample active structure with varying material parameters. The results showed that the proposed method could accurately determine the material parameter within a reasonable range, meeting the requirements for its use in active structures with an attached acoustic chamber.

Within the easiest scoto-seesaw framework, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, dark matter phenomena, and neutrino oscillations. By integrating the radiative neutrino model with the hidden sector, we address both light dark matter and heavy neutrinos, ensuring the stability of the proton and the dark matter particle. Furthermore, we evaluate the minimal values for the high-scale invisible and visible dark parity breaking scales, determining that the hidden sector particle most likely decays before the onset of electroweak symmetry breaking. Utilizing the one-loop correction to the S$_{1}$, a gauge singlet field, we calculate the impact of the hidden sector on the self-interaction term of the S$_{1}$ potential, ensuring the stability of the vacuum even in the extreme limit of strong hidden sector symmetry breaking.
